title: The hidden supply chain costs of the AI boom
summary: Today, I’m talking with Willy Shih, an economist, a professor of management practice at Harvard Business School, and the author of the upcoming book, Where Does My Stuff Come From? The Powerful Economics Behind Global Supply Chains. Willy is one of my all-time favorite Decoder guests — his way of looking at the world through […]
content: Today, I’m talking with Willy Shih, an economist, a professor of management practice at Harvard Business School, and the author of the upcoming book, Where Does My Stuff Come From? The Powerful Economics Behind Global Supply Chains . Willy is one of my all-time favorite Decoder guests — his way of looking at the world through our supply chains is just a fascinating way of making sense of the global economy. I first met Willy in 2019, while The Verge was covering Foxconn’s promise to build an LCD fab in Wisconsin. That obviously never happened, but Willy called it right away because he could see the supply chain to support a fab simply wasn’t in place. We also had Willy on the show in 2021 to talk about what was then the pandemic-era chip shortage. Now, five years later, we’re in another manufacturing mess, as we stand in the middle of a political fight over whether globalization is coming to an end. Trumps’ tariffs keep changing, the factories that were supposed to reshore in America mostly haven’t materialized, and AI is devouring the planet’s computing resources during an unprecedented infrastructure buildout. Willy’s new book is all about the economics underlying these complex systems, which our politicians and regulators seem to insistently ignore. You’ll hear us talk about why the markets have reacted to all these disruptions the way they have, and why China remains a global manufacturing powerhouse even though every other country thinks that’s so risky. I loved this conversation — it’s in the weeds, and Willy really knows his stuff. Okay: economist Will Shih on his new book Where Does My Stuff Come From? Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Willy Shih, you’re an economist and professor of management practice at Harvard. You’re also the author of the new book, Where Does My Stuff Come From: The Powerful Economics Behind Global Supply Chains . Welcome back to Decoder . Well, thanks for having me back. I am very excited to talk to you. You and I first started talking ages ago when The Verge was covering Foxconn in Wisconsin. You are a reliable source of information on what it takes to actually build an LCD plant anywhere, not just in Wisconsin. The Foxconn in Wisconsin thing was funny because I tend to go on first principles on these things. Once I knew they weren’t going to build a glass plant across the street, it’s like there’s no way there’s going to be a factory. Now, what happened afterwards, of course, is people heard your show, and then I started getting calls from people who live in the community. They went to the zoning hearings in town, then sent me the plans and asked, “Is this going to be a panel factory?” I said, “No, I told you it’s not going to be a panel factory.” So they sent me the plans. I said, “Well, there’s not enough concrete to make this a panel factory.” For a panel factory, you need stability, so you gotta have all this structural steel, and you have to have all this concrete. Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here . Not a subscriber? You can sign up here . My favorite part of the Foxconn story — and I don’t mean to rehash it, but it’s just fun to talk to you about it again — is when you said there’s not enough concrete and steel. It’s great. We should actually talk about LCD manufacturing a little bit. There’s an entire chapter in your book about why all of it is in China and China’s investment in that. But I want to just take a big step back for a second. It seems to me that you’ve written a book about the end of globalization in one particular way. We had big global supply chains. The pandemic came and shocked the just-in-time manufacturing system to its core. And then the Trump administration, in the second round, has imposed a whole bunch of tariffs. I’ve had several guests on the show straightforwardly tell me we’re de-globalizing the economy. That’s what’s happening here. We can’t rely on it anymore. Your book, as you read it, is a little bit of a reaction to that, but you’re also pointing out how globalization is one of the smartest ways to do it based on first principles of economics. Tell me about the state of the world and the state of our supply chains right now from your point of view. Well, I think the point about first principles of economics is actually spot on. I often tell people my father was an economist, and I used to see him come home from work, and I thought, “I never want to do that. I’m going to go into science and technology.” So I went into science and technology and took all these engineering classes. And I was in product businesses only to discover, to my horror, that if you don’t get the economics right, then it doesn’t matter for science and technology. The book’s subtitle is “the powerful economics behind global supply chains.” I talk about all these principles behind global supply chains, but they’re all actually driven by economics. In fact, what you see today is market forces responding to all this stuff. So, for example, when we put tariffs on stuff coming out of China, then manufacturers say, “Okay, let me move that supply chain, and I’ll do my assembly in Vietnam, or I’m going to do my assembly in Mexico, or let me find some way to circumvent these tariffs.” What I really find is that when you look at how these supply chains are structured, like why do cashew nuts say they come from Vietnam when they were actually grown in the Ivory Coast or Ghana? Well, there was an economic reason for all of these things. It’s why frozen fish that are caught off the coast of Alaska go to Qingdao, China, for processing before they come back. Again, it’s because it’s cheaper to do it that way. When we put up these trade barriers, the first reaction tends to be, “How can I circumvent that?” We saw a lot of that, especially last year. I remember Liberation Day was April 2nd, and if you look at the quarter right before, people knew stuff was going to be happening. We have this circumvention going. That’s why in the first quarter of 2025, we had all-time-record imports from Ireland, and then the first half of 2026 showed slow imports from Ireland. That’s because we’re burning off all the stuff we imported in the first half of 2025. It all gets down to economics. I’m getting all these TV set ads because the holiday season is coming up. Great, and they’re all coming from Mexico. It’s like, “How can they all be coming from Mexico?” I know the flat panel factories that supply all these TV sets these days are all in China, and they’re all in China because the plants have been subsidized so heavily or because of industrial policies that have encouraged those plants to be there. If you watch the trade lanes, you’ll see this stuff. What happens is there’ve been all these new shipping routes from China to Mexico over the last two years. Direct ocean container service from China to Mexico. It’s like, “Huh, I wonder what that’s about.” I’ll tell you what it’s about. It’s about moving parts and components from China to Mexico so that I can assemble them in Mexico and then bring them in under the USMCA agreement. So what you’re actually seeing is that these supply chains are organized the way they are partly because some places have the capabilities, but more often than not, a lot of these are just responding to economic forces. If I’m going to add on tariffs or I’m going to make it more expensive to ship something between two points, the market will find a way around that. That’s something I want to come back to several times in this conversation. “It’s cheaper” was a real driving force of globalization. Americans like cheap things. They like cheap flat-panel TVs. The fact that I can go to Costco right now and get a 50-inch TV for $300 is a miracle of the modern supply chain and of modern manufacturing. It is a miracle, right? And it’s cheaper, and it’s because there’s a place that, for better or for worse, can make it cheaper. By the way, American consumers benefit from that. One of the reasons that we pursued free trade and globalization so heavily in the United States is that we thought that creating economic ties between all these various countries would reduce the potential for an armed conflict. There are a lot of ways to think about that, but in general, if you tie the economies together, the price of having a war shoots up, and then you won’t have free or cheap TVs, and maybe the public won’t like that. That is under pressure now, right? We’re sitting here in the middle of an AI conversation, where China is routinely invoked as the great threat that will rise up if they get to AGI before us. We are putting up tariffs, particularly on China. In the United States, the policy administration is to bring manufacturing back to the United States through the use of tariffs. Your point of view is that simple economics will provide enough contortions to avoid that blunt outcome. When we seal the borders for some products everywhere, then the price is going to go up. So, for example, putting tariffs on steel. Initially, when we just put tariffs on imported steel and aluminum, then what happened was, “Well, gee, I happen to be making construction equipment. More than half of the cost of that construction equipment is medium carbon steel, so therefore it makes it easier for me to import construction equipment from somewhere else.” We then say, “Okay. Now we’re going to tariff stuff based on your steel content.” Eventually, when you close off all those things, which means you’re basically tariffing everything, then stuff gets more expensive domestically. You could look back on the period from 2000 until really 2012 to 2014; we had relatively low inflation. Part of it is because we were getting cheaper stuff from China. I think there are a couple of things that drove a breakdown of this model, if you will. One is that people didn’t really recognize that the connection between moving work out of the US to China meant you’re leaving people behind who don’t have any more work. That cost was spread over people who, by the way, also shop at Walmart and benefit from the cheap goods. But we as a country didn’t think about it like, how are we going to retrain all those people who weren’t making furniture in North Carolina or who were making castings and forgings in Kentucky or wherever? That was one part of the problem. The other part of the problem is that we have this gigantic trade deficit. Now, a lot of that is fueled by government spending and borrowing and so on. But typically, in some respects, you would’ve expected the exchange rate or some other adjustment mechanism to compensate for that. I remember the last time exchange rates moved was in the 1980s. That was also the last time the US ever had a trade surplus, when the dollar got a lot cheaper relative to the Japanese yen, especially at that time. That had an adjustment on trade flows as well. So now you have China running this ginormous trade surplus. Basically, what they’re doing is exporting their economic problems in China to the US, and they’re exporting that at the expense of jobs elsewhere. The Europeans have suddenly woken up to that. Now go to a place like Germany, where half the economy revolves around the auto industry, and they now have figured it out, and it’s like, “Wait a minute, this is an existential crisis for us.” But on those two things, the controls you would’ve expected to rebalance things didn’t pan out. That’s why we have so much discussion about this right now and a view of this as a problem. It feels like my entire teen experience was a conversation about NAFTA, and we should open free trade in North America. Later on, I got to college, and all the economic discussion was about the EU and creating the single market in the EU: “We’re going to set up these big open markets, and there’s going to be free trade inside of those markets, and that will lead to a kind of economic prosperity.” Fast forward to 2026, and the desire to tear a lot of that down has gone way up, right? Particularly as you look at the USMCA and Chinese goods coming to Mexico to come to the United States, nakedly circumventing the entire policy goal of imposing tariffs. The goal is to build the iPhone in the United States. The goal is to build manufacturing in the United States. I know that you have never really thought that’s an achievable goal, but that is the goal. That is what the administration promised. We’ve created these trade groups, trade associations, that allow that goal to be circumvented. Do you think the walls are going to keep going up, or do you think they’re going to come back down? I think we’re going to see more pressure to moderate our behavior a little bit because, let’s face it, there are a lot of goods that we, as a country, need access to inexpensive labor. So I’m actually very pro-USMCA as a successor to NAFTA because I actually think there are things that we need inexpensive labor for. Mexico is a good place to source things like that. There are things that we need from Canada. So if we were to look at North America as a trading bloc, then what you would see is the benefits of specialization, which is the whole rationale for trade in the first place. We’re better at doing this, you’re better at doing that; you specialize in that, we’ll specialize in this. We trade; everybody is better off. If you can do that with a community of countries that understand the need for that type of balance, then everybody is better off. I think the problem with China is they’re very happy to have this imbalance, where they want the world to be dependent on them, but they don’t want to buy stuff from the rest of the world. When you have that, then trade doesn’t really work. So I think that’s the problem. I’m hoping we’re going to realize that we’re better off among a group of like-minded countries where we can trade within that bloc. So for example, if the US were to view North American partners and European partners in Japan — and countries in Southeast Asia, Australia, New Zealand, parts of Central and South America, and even Africa — and say, “Okay, let’s trade across this bloc,” then we’d have access to most of what we need, whether it’s critical minerals, low-cost labor, or a lot of technology specialties. We could do much better with that, much better than a go-it-alone strategy in my view. The first part of your book — which I highly recommend the audience read; it’s a fun read — is just setting up the first principles of why we trade at all in the very concept of labor arbitrage. It seems like we’re having a national policy conversation that is 500 steps removed from these basic ideas of why we would trade. It is entirely centered around: can you bring manufacturing back to America because we let all the manufacturing jobs go to Mexico and China, particularly in high tech? And we’re behind. There might be some extraordinarily bad event, like a war, where it’s exposed how little manufacturing capability we have in the United States. That has nothing to do with the basics of specialization in various countries around the world. It’s another problem, and the blunt instrument is, “Boy, it’s bad that all of our drones are made in China. We’re going to prevent drones from being sold here. Of course, our industry will set up drone manufacturing in the United States.” I don’t see that connection. Do you see that working? No. I think that’s a transactional view where you look at one piece at a time as opposed to looking at the bigger picture. I think we have to start with a core principle that the US is a high-cost country. Therefore, if you want manufacturing jobs coming to the US, then you’ve got to have high labor productivity. In fact, if you look at the types of jobs that are coming back to the US, they tend to use a lot of automation, a lot of sophisticated manufacturing processes, and stuff that is high-skill that can justify the high labor cost. Either that, or they are things where we have a technological lead that nobody else knows how to do in the world. I was looking at the high-temperature superalloys that are used in the hot section of jet engines. There are only three companies in the world that know how to cast those, and two of them are in the US, and one of them is in the UK. There are things like that the rest of the world has to buy from us. So if you have high labor productivity or highly differentiated products, those we can make in the US; we can make them successfully. By the way, most of them never left the country. The US, France, and the UK are major suppliers of jet engines to the entire world market. Even the Chinese buy those from the West. So if we have these things that we do better than anybody else, we should invest in those and make sure that we’re always in the lead, and then everybody else will buy from us, and then you’ll have some balance where you can’t be held up. There’s a lot of this thinking like, “I wish I could turn the clock back to the 1980s or the 1970s, when manufacturing was the path to the middle class in the US.” But manufacturing has changed worldwide, and for those jobs that you want to have manufacturing in the US, you’ve got to have high labor productivity or the high differentiation that’ll go with it. I want to stay on the iPhone for one more second. Apple just inked a new deal where they’re going to source a bunch of titanium from a Pennsylvania-based company called Perryman for the iPhone 18 Pro and the new iPhone Duo. They’re going to source that titanium here. They’re then going to ship it to China. They’re going to assemble the phone in China, and they’re going to ship the phones back to us. They do that with Corning and glass as well. I’ve always looked at that. Tim Cook’s job, in particular, is that he’s a statesman. He has to negotiate with Donald Trump and Xi Jinping about iPhone production and tariffs in these supply chains, and the iPhone holds the global economy together. If the price of the iPhone gets too high because of tariffs, maybe there’s an electoral impact in the United States. How do you see products like that? Are they as load-bearing as it feels to me, or are they just examples of the larger system? I think the iPhone is a terrific example of how difficult this problem is. Because right now you have components that have high technological complexity. The iPhone uses the most advanced chips produced by Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company. By the way, most of those chips are still going to be made in Taiwan. TSMC has a fab in Arizona, but its capacity is piddly compared to what it has in Taiwan. Those chips come from one place and require the most sophisticated processing tools that come from ASML in the Netherlands, but also companies like Lam Research and Applied Materials in the US. So it’s that global thing. But the key thing is iPhones also require assembly labor. They require manual assembly because we’re not at the point yet where you can assemble the whole thing with a robot. There’s actually a chapter in my book where I talk about what Henry Ford and the lifestyles of the Chinese Communist Party have to do with assembling iPhones. It turns out it’s a lot. The lifestyles of the Chinese Communist Party have to do with how they mobilize workers in what’s called the Danwei model , which was established after the Communist Revolution. It’s where you have a production site, a walled city with housing for workers, a means of production, warehouses, ways to feed them, and stuff like that. If you ever go to a phone factory in China, the real question is: how do I mobilize 100,000 to 200,000 workers to do this manual assembly on a scale that an Apple needs? They’re trying to do it in India. They’re having some success with India, but that was really hard. Once again, it’s: how do I mobilize manual labor at that level of scale? So the iPhone, as you point out, is a great example of a global product because it needs the highest level of tech, and it also needs the huge workforce to do the manual assembly. There’s actually a great book called Apple in China , which I also recommend. The narrative is that the Chinese government subsidized an awful lot of manufacturing in China. They built these cities, and they built the culture that enables the labor at scale. Your example in the book, again, is LCD factories, where the Chinese government invested in overcapacity, and that drove the price of LCD manufacturing down. Basically, it’s all centered in China now. The flip side of that is, boy, it’s pretty obvious that they stole a bunch of American intellectual property along the way. They developed these manufacturing capabilities. They took a lot of the know-how that Apple imported into that country. They did the same with Tesla in a lot of ways. They stood up an entire electric car industry on the back of the innovation Tesla had started through manufacturing in that country. Now they have those capabilities, and they’re racing ahead of our companies because we don’t actually have the manufacturing know-how. Can you rebalance that? I hear this concern a lot: that you can’t rebalance it. If all the manufacturing happens there, they will actually be state-of-the-art, and we will fall behind. I’m not sure if “stole” is the best description of how they got these capabilities. I would say they learned it, and in many cases we taught it to them. Being a supplier to Apple is often referred to as a golden ticket, and people say, “Well, why is it a golden ticket?” Well, obviously you get cash flow from selling products to them. But the other thing is that Apple is a real taskmaster. By making you work hard to improve your products, improve your specs, meet their performance specs, and meet their cost targets, you get better. The same thing happened when Tesla set up their factory in Shanghai. The fact that they qualified local suppliers raised the game in the Chinese EV market. Another thing I think a lot of people miss about China is that there is actually this very interesting competition going on. Beijing sets policies and objectives, but then all the regional governments, the provinces, and the major cities are competing with each other. They set up this free market dynamic, and so you have this fierce competition between regions. The regions are also very smart about setting objectives. They keep raising the bar for people so the technology gets better. You have a dynamic where there’s really cutthroat competition in the Chinese market, and it’s about survival to make better products at lower prices. That’s something that’s really driving it right now. To your point about how, to the extent we’ve lost the ability to make things, the Chinese have a lot of capabilities. You should walk through some Chinese factories these days. They’re way ahead of the US in terms of using automation, because they’re investing like crazy. I had a student I was talking to about his father’s factory in Shanghai, and he said his father’s answer to everything, every competitive threat, was just more CapEx: “I’m going to throw more capital at it. I’m going to buy the latest machine.” I was in one factory a couple of months ago where the equipment was two or maybe three years old, and they were ripping it out and upgrading it to the latest generation because they said, “This is how we’re going to survive. We have to make the product more efficiently, and we have to make a better product.” So there’s this internal competition in the Chinese marketplace that is really fearsome, and it’s hard for Western companies to compete there, but that is an important dynamic that’s going on as well. The interesting thing about that, as I compare and contrast China with the United States, is that the system in China is understood. It’s stable. You can make a lot of criticisms of that system. I think you can make an endless number of human rights criticisms of the Chinese government. It’s obviously a repressive government in a lot of ways. But the economic system is understood, and it’s controlled at the top in a meaningfully stable way. The goals are apparent, the investment is apparent, and there’s a lot of competition to achieve those goals with that investment. There are two things about that which I think are significant. The first is that China engages in long-term planning, five-year plans. Now, when I was a kid, I used to look at China’s five-year plans, and I thought, “This is a big joke,” because they would make a lot of mistakes, like Mao Zedong’s Great Leap Forward, and they were doing this new type of tillage in farming, and they caused this huge famine and millions of people died. But to the credit of the government there, when they do this type of long-range planning, they learn from their mistakes, and they get better. If you look at their current five-year plans and the last couple of five-year plans, they’re good plans. They understand what’s important, and they focus on those things that are important. Then the second point is about what kinds of people they have implementing these plans. I was in one of these third-tier cities some number of years ago, and I was having dinner with the economic development commission there. At the beginning of dinner, I said, “Hey guys, just for fun, let’s go around the table and talk about what you studied in school.” It was mechanical engineering, industrial engineering, electrical engineering, metallurgy, metallurgy, mechanical engineering. You go to Washington and ask what people studied in school, and it’s political science, economics, and government. So you have these technocrats competing in technology-intensive businesses and having that understanding. By the way, that’s one of the reasons I wrote this book: I was serving on these committees appointed by the Commerce Secretary on supply chains, and I realized we have civil servants who don’t have the exposure to supply chains and how stuff is actually made. China had this plan that was called the 863 plan . The 863 plan was when four scholars went to the government in Beijing in March of 1986 — that’s why it’s called “863”; it was ‘86, March. I remember the first time I looked at the 863 plan, and it was, “If we want to be a modern economy, we have to be good at these things.” I looked at that plan in the 1990s, and I said, “This is a good plan.” And they’ve executed every one of those things. They said, “We need to be good at all these things, like information technology, biotechnology.” In semiconductors, they still have a way to go, but they identified civil aircraft. But they identified all these different technologies like communications technology, software, and robotics. I would contrast that with the Trump administration here in Trump’s second term, where… We already talked about Liberation Day. Howard Lutnick is on television saying, “We’re going to move manufacturing back to the United States. This is the goal of the tariffs.” Three weeks later, there are 900 lawsuits about the tariffs, and Howard Lutnick is back on TV saying, “Robots will do all the manufacturing now. This is the goal. We’re going to do heavy automation.” And then the tariffs get struck down, and they find a new law for different tariffs. It does not seem like the same long-term planning that can be stuck to, or the same environment where businesses understand the stability of the trading system such that they can compete ferociously. Every CEO who does manufacturing and comes on the show usually ends up talking to me about how they scrambled to buy RAM at affordable prices to make their products, which has to keep them from doing anything else. How would you contrast that? Can we get out of this moment where it’s a pure scramble, or is this fully shaking everything up? We’re in a very transactional environment. Everything is short-term, and these rapid changes that you see in the tariffs… If you look at a map of 2025 and 2026 and put a dot everywhere there was some tariff action, it looks like a shotgun hit the wall. There are all these spots all over the place. The problem with that is when you have that type of instability, it’s very hard for a company to make any long-term plans. Before I build a factory, I want to know that I’m going to have stable demand for a couple of years, at least until I have a chance of earning a return on that thing. I’ve talked to a couple of companies about this. These were overseas companies thinking about coming into the US market, and they said, “Well, I can’t do it because things keep changing. Do I go to Mexico? Do I go to the US? What part of the US do I go into?” Especially with things like semiconductor fabs, you need to know that you’re going to be able to get 10 to 20 years out of it. When things change every couple of weeks, what that does instead is say, “I’m just going to hold off on an investment because it’s just too uncertain. It changes too often.” Are you seeing that slow down in investment? Are you seeing companies say, “We can’t actually invest in manufacturing in the United States”? It varies. I see that with a lot of companies asking, “Where do I want to put my production operations?” Okay, now we see some things like car plants coming into the US, and usually that’s a function of the pain being too great. But the whole auto tariff thing is also a little bit crazy. If you look historically at production strategies in the auto industry, typically when you build a plant, you size it to build about 200,000 to 250,000 units of a model or a model family, because that’s like the efficient scale for an auto plant. Then what you have is a company like BMW that says, “Great, I’m going to build all my X Series SUVs in South Carolina. I’ll build the 3 Series somewhere else. I’ll build the 5 Series somewhere else, and I’ll build the 7 Series somewhere else. And then what I’ll do is exchange them.” So BMW in South Carolina or Mercedes in Alabama, they build certain models in the US, export them to the rest of the world, and then import other models so that you have the whole product line. Toyota does that. For example, they build more Camrys in the US than anywhere else, and they were exporting some of those as well. But then when you start putting tariffs on imports, that screws up that whole strategy. Again, it’s a decision that was made without understanding how the automakers had laid out that strategy.. You need to understand how the supply chain is structured and why it’s structured the way it is, and then you can be more thoughtful.. Do you see tariffs as mostly protectionist? I was in France earlier this year, and I took an Uber, and I think it was a BYD Seal, a Chinese EV. I asked the French Uber driver, “How do you like this car?” He was very French, and he literally did the thing. He goes, “Peugeot is shit.” I almost started clapping because it was amazing. He’s like, “If the French government would just allow the Chinese government to sell these cars here, these companies would all be dead.” In the United States, I think Jim Farley, the CEO of Ford, is running around saying the Chinese EVs are superior to American products. It’s the tariffs that protect our markets and protect our manufacturers, because you could import the cars, but you’d pay such high tariffs that they’re economically infeasible. That’s just pure protectionism. That goes against what you’re saying, which is that you need to protect your industry until their products are good enough to compete on the global scale. But we’re not doing that with our carmakers. We’re just protecting them. Yeah, and there’s a cost associated with that. So, for example, one of the famous tariffs is a so-called chicken tax. I talk about this in the book as well. The chicken tax resulted from this trade spat where we put tariffs on imported light trucks. SUVs are built on that platform. It’s one of the reasons the Detroit automakers have focused on SUVs and light trucks. That’s their profit center because there’ve been tariffs on that, and it’s only happened in the last decade or so that Toyota and Nissan and others have made more light trucks in the US and Mexico. So that’s one of the results of that type of tariff distortion. Wait. But that’s a policy victory, right? Toyota, Nissan, and all the other foreign manufacturers are going to make trucks in the United States. You’ve gotten some economic benefit; they can compete, and maybe all the trucks are going to get better. You get some economic benefit, but one of the reasons the Detroit guys still make so many trucks and SUVs on those platforms is because they’re more profitable, which says the price is higher than it might otherwise have been. But I do see the benefit of that. Although I have to say, I was walking around the Toyota factory in Georgetown, Kentucky. I’m walking around with the plant manager, and I said, “You’re making sedans here?” He said, “Yep,” and a lot of the Detroit guys have given up making sedans because they can’t make any money. I said, “And you’re using parts that mostly come from Kentucky, Ohio, Indiana, Alabama, Mississippi, and Texas, and some from Mexico and Japan, but mostly domestic content.” He’s like, “Yep.” I said, “And you’re using American workers.” He said, “Yep.” I said, “You’re using American-made steel.” I’m trying to get out of him that, okay, look, I know American steel costs a lot more than imported steel because I’ve been in other factories that are still importing steel despite the steel tariffs because they say it’s still cheaper in Asia. But I said, “You’re using American-made steel.” So I’m trying to get that out of him: how much he’s paying for steel. Obviously, he’s not going to tell me, but he does say, “We have a strategic long-term relationship with our supplier.” That tells you a lot, which is that there are ways you can do these things. You have to work with your suppliers. You have to give them longer-term arrangements, be less transactional, more strategic on things like that. So I think you can do it, but it really takes a comprehensive and more thoughtful approach. I understand the rationale for putting tariffs on foreign goods that undercut our markets. You’re just going to increase the cost, and then maybe the consumer will buy the domestic product, and that’s better for our economy. It just hasn’t seemed to have worked. I don’t see Liberation Day as having done anything except generally raise prices on everything. We haven’t actually remapped the global economy. And a lot of what you’re describing is, well, the system is pretty resilient. The system was pretty resilient to COVID. The system was pretty resilient to an oil tanker getting stuck in the Suez Canal. The system has been pretty resilient to the war in Iran. The system has been pretty resilient to absolutely chaotic tariffs. Maybe some prices have risen, and I’m sure we’re going to get listeners pointing out that all the prices have risen. It feels like the only thing the system isn’t resilient to is the AI industry wanting every scrap of RAM that the whole world can produce. And so now there’s not going to be inexpensive cell phones. What will push the system over the breaking point? Because globalization has seemed generally resilient to a bunch of people who want it to be over. I think what you’re highlighting is that it’s really the power of the market. In the case of closing the Strait of Hormuz, Brent North Sea crude prices didn’t go to $150 a barrel like I was afraid they would, and a lot of people were afraid they would because the market adjusted. We applied a lot of tariffs on Liberation Day. The first response was circumvention or front-running. The next response was tariff engineering. The next response is like, “Okay, let me move production to Vietnam or let me move production to Mexico, and I’ll find a way around that.” Now, eventually, when you close down all those things, then prices eventually have to rise. In the case of memory chips, that’s a different problem because the demand far outstripped the capacity. I used to always buy memory cards on Black Friday. Forget that this year. Yeah, it’s all over. I’m just glad I stocked up on a previous Black Friday. If you want to know my prediction for when the AI industry will meet its true political end, it’s when Grand Theft Auto VI comes out. Everyone goes out to buy a PS5, and they realize it’s more expensive now at the end of its life cycle than it was at the beginning because the price of memory has skyrocketed. Yeah, no kidding. We’re talking about huge amounts. But that’s the same thing. We’re in a phase where we see all these tactical actions taken by the government, very transactional, without necessarily understanding all the complex interconnections and interdependencies. You may have noticed, for example, that the administration temporarily suspended the Jones Act. I don’t know if you remember that. Why did they temporarily suspend the Jones Act? Because oil refineries on the East Coast of the US couldn’t get their oil from Texas cheaply because there were no domestic supertankers. The Jones Act requires that if you move stuff from Texas to New Jersey, you have to have a US-owned, US-crewed, US-built, very large crude carrier. There aren’t any because we don’t build those in the US. So that’s why it’s cheaper to bring oil from Algeria to New Jersey than it is to bring it from Texas. And that’s why they suspended the Jones Act for a while. At least they understood that. I know at least some of our audience is going to be listening to this conversation, and you’re steeped in global trade. You wrote a book to educate our government about how it works from the basics, which I think is sorely needed. But a lot of the promise for young people in our politics lately is that we will rebuild American capacity. We will rebuild manufacturing capacity. We will bring back a bunch of jobs where you don’t need an advanced degree in AI prompt engineering or whatever to see the future. We will bring back the dignity of work. Politicians on both sides are making these promises all the time, and a lot of that requires closing down trade, forcing that economic activity back within our borders. It just seems like that isn’t likely. So I’m not going to ask you whether or not that is totally likely. I’m going to ask: what’s more likely instead? Well, I think what’s more likely is that we will see efforts as you describe. I would love to sit down with people and say, okay, we want to move this type of production back to the US. Let’s take a more strategic, more nuanced approach, understanding the bigger picture, considering what levers are available. The US is still a big, attractive market. It is the largest market in the world. It is the most attractive market in the world. That’s, by the way, why the Chinese all want to come here: because they can make some money here that they can’t make elsewhere. So then how do we harness that market power and that market pull with a more nuanced understanding of why our supply chains are organized the way they are today? Recognizing that, can I build a strategy to bring important things that are very strategic for the US to know how to do? Let’s think about how we fix this problem with an understanding of that bigger picture. Willy, it’s been great to talk to you. It is always just a pleasure. We have to have you back faster than five years. Thank you so much for being on Decoder . Thanks for having me. Questions or comments? Hit us up at decoder@theverge.com. We really do read every email!

content: Top of the morning to you. Gray skies are hovering over the Pharmalot campus right now, but our spirits remain sunny, nonetheless. Why? We will trot out a bit of insight from the Morning Mayor, who would say “Every new day should be unwrapped like a precious gift.” So while you tug on the ribbon, we will celebrate the notion by brewing still more cups of stimulation. As always, you are invited you to join us. Our choice today is strawberry creme. Meanwhile, here are a few items of interest. Hope you have a smashing day and, of course, do stay in touch. … The number of investigator-initiated trials, a Chinese regulatory pathway that allowed investigators to start clinical trials without sign-off from central regulators, have slowed considerably , STAT reports. Loosened rules had enabled Chinese companies to test drugs in humans faster and cheaper and prompted U.S. companies to either come to China or push the U.S. Food and Drug Administration to adopt a similar approach. But since May, when the Chinese government issued new restrictions, 164 have been approved under the new regulations and just over 1,000 were submitted for review. India proposed rules requiring regulators to immediately suspend manufacturing licenses for medicines that fail specified quality standards in government testing, tightening oversight of one of the world’s biggest ​pharmaceutical industries , Reuters writes. The rules would apply if government testing finds the drug fails quality standards for impurities ‌or sterility, the amount of active ingredient, or dissolution, which assesses how the drug releases that ingredient. The license would remain suspended until the ​manufacturer conducts an effective root-cause analysis and implements corrective and preventive action, and could be restored only after regulators verify those measures have been implemented. Texas was the new epicenter of the AI data center buildout. That might be kaput. Texas is the fastest-growing data center market in the US and ground zero for Big Tech’s largest AI buildouts. But the blue wave that swept the Lone Star State may jeopardize that position. Democrat James Talarico won the US Senate seat, Gina Hinojosa won the race for governor, and Democrats will take control of the Texas House for the first time in 24 years. They won after making data centers a central issue on the campaign trail. The swings could spell trouble for hyperscalers with ambitious plans in the state. They also add to growing anxiety that America’s AI buildout could stall. Here’s how the election results could reshape AI’s future . —James O’Donnell What’s next for US energy policy after the midterm elections? Democrats have taken control of both the House and the Senate, but we probably won’t see major federal climate and energy legislation while Trump remains president. The midterm elections could, however, be a big deal for energy at the state and local level. The results could shape everything from the state grid and data center development to renewable energy and greenhouse gas emissions. The long-rumored Motorola Signature 27 is real, featuring top-of-the-line specs, a super-bright OLED screen, and a ton of cameras. But all this high-end hardware won't come cheap in the age of AI. Motorola's new flagship smartphone will run a whopping $1,600 when it arrives later this month. The Signature 27 is a completely new take on flagship smartphones from Motorola, leaving behind the middling legacy of the Edge series. However, you'll still immediately clock this as a Motorola device due to its distinctive use of materials and Pantone colors. The phone is metal, ceramic, and glass, but the backs are textured polycarbonate. The device comes in Coal Smoke (black) or Capulet Olive (green) colors. The former has a "tactical weave" finish inspired by automotive design, and the latter is "textile-inspired." This device will include the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6, the most powerful mobile chip Qualcomm offers right now. While some smartphones have flirted with 16GB of memory, that's less common these days. The Signature 27 will have 12GB like Samsung's base model flagships. However, there's not going to be an upgrade option for more. You will, however, get a generous 512GB of storage. Read full article Comments

title: STAT+: In China, a flood of controversial clinical trials slows to a trickle
summary: Following patient deaths, China restricts investigator-initiated biotech trials, leaving rare disease families and US investors facing an uncertain future.
content: SHANGHAI — Juan Huang noticed her 13-year-old daughter, Huangxi, was leaning out of her stroller, so she undid the buckles, scooped her out, and laid the length of her — long, loose, rail thin — across her lap. In 2014, doctors here had no answers for why 16-month-old Huangxi suddenly couldn’t stand or walk anymore. It took two years and a flight to Massachusetts to diagnose a genetic disease never identified in China, and even the Boston Children’s Hospital doctors couldn’t offer any treatments. But much has changed in the decade since. Chinese hospitals became sophisticated centers for diagnosing and treating rare disease. And a foundation Huang works for helped push genetic treatments into trials, at a fraction of the cost in the U.S. It was on track to start two more trials — until this summer, when deaths, news reports , and new government rules upended those plans. The government has become “very strict,” she said, as she stroked Huangxi’s back on a bench on the banks of the Huangpu River. Huang, who worked as an engineer before her daughter’s diagnosis, and her Hope for Rare Foundation were pursuing investigator-initiated trials (IIT), a Chinese regulatory pathway that allowed investigators to start clinical trials without sign-off from central regulators. The loosened rules enabled Chinese companies to test drugs in humans faster and cheaper and prompted U.S. companies to either come to China or push the Food and Drug Administration to adopt a similar approach. title: New WHO technical package to help countries improve health data for COVID-19 response and beyond
summary: Today, as part of its commitment to strengthening health information systems and improving health[1], especially in the context of the COVID-19 pandemic, WHO announced a new approach to improving access to life-saving data: the SCORE for Health Data Technical Package. The COVID-19 pandemic has highlighted the urgent need for timely and reliable data to drive strategic health action. Too many count
content: Today, as part of its commitment to strengthening health information systems and improving health[1], especially in the context of the COVID-19 pandemic, WHO announced a new approach to improving access to life-saving data: the SCORE for Health Data Technical Package. The COVID-19 pandemic has highlighted the urgent need for timely and reliable data to drive strategic health action. Too many countries still lack both the infrastructure to routinely gather health data and the analytical capacity to use these data for effective health actions and emergency response. “Countries must be able to measure progress to make progress,” said WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus. “Particularly during COVID-19, reliable data is the best way to coordinate response efforts and improve health in all areas.” Accurate health data are necessary to understand specific country needs in order to improve health and save lives. Data also helps direct scarce resources to where they are needed most. The SCORE (Survey, Count, Optimize, Review, Enable) Technical Package aims to improve the availability of timely, reliable, validated, and comparable health data. For the first time in a single, harmonized package, it represents all the key elements for optimized health information system performance. Simply put, SCORE will help governments around the globe set benchmarks and improve standards in healthcare. In response to the challenges of data availability highlighted in the WHO World Health Statistics 2020 report, SCORE includes more than 90 universally-accepted tools and standards for health information systems strengthening. “Using data to inform public health priorities and strategies has never been more important,” said Dr Kelly Henning, Director of Public Health Programs at Bloomberg Philanthropies[2]. “The SCORE Technical Package provides country governments around the world with high-quality, essential technical guidance so that countries can strengthen their own data systems.” WHO is proud to partner with the Bloomberg Philanthropies Data for Health Initiative to deliver this timely resource to countries. Below are some examples of how SCORE can improve individual lives and communities: The birth of a child is registered so they can access essential health services, attend school, and apply for a passport; A death is registered with cause-of-death accurately captured so that policy-makers have a better understanding of all-cause and COVID-specific mortality and associated risk factors and implement programs and policies to save lives; Health data are disaggregated by age, sex and cause of death to illustrate the root causes of health disparities and help direct resources to the most vulnerable groups such as those who do not speak the local language or face stigma and discrimination in their community; Health facilities have the capacity to regularly measure the quality of their services, workforce and patient data and can make a compelling case for increased funding to national and international stakeholders; Health data are integrated with other sectors so that social determinants of health such as pollution, sanitation and nutrition are addressed to reduce the overall burden of disease. The package's initial release includes two documents: SCORE Essential Interventions – including an overview of health information systems, underlying elements, and indicators to assess progress with sample actions; and SCORE Tools and Standards -- including resources to address critical health data gaps and strengthen country health data. “We must keep score to save lives. WHO is committed to working with countries and partners to rapidly scale up capacity for data collection and use in order to improve policy and performance,” added Dr Samira Asma, Assistant Director-General for Data, Analytics and Delivery for Impact at WHO. “We must act now to invest in statistical systems in countries, respond to this pandemic and meet the SDGs and the Triple Billion targets. Our window of opportunity is closing, and we cannot wait to address data gaps. Data use to address country needs has to be a priority today.” Country-owned, disaggregated data will be essential for more resilient and sustainable health systems going forward. COVID-19 is both a wake-up call and a stark reminder of the challenges we still have to address. But it is also an opportunity to build back better through solidarity, information-sharing and collaboration. SCORE is one example of how a collaborative approach can benefit countries by providing a common set of tools based on shared standards. This package is designed to be practical, actionable and flexible. We will only be successful in combatting COVID-19 if we work together. Future components of the SCORE Technical Package are due to be released later this year, including the SCORE Assessment Instrument and global, regional and country status reports. summary: The COVID-19 pandemic has disrupted or halted critical mental health services in 93% of countries worldwide while the demand for mental health is increasing, according to a new WHO survey. content: The COVID-19 pandemic has disrupted or halted critical mental health services in 93% of countries worldwide while the demand for mental health is increasing, according to a new WHO survey. The survey of 130 countries provides the first global data showing the devastating impact of COVID-19 on access to mental health services and underscores the urgent need for increased funding. The survey was published ahead of WHO’s Big Event for Mental Health ̶ a global online advocacy event on 10 October that will bring together world leaders, celebrities, and advocates to call for increased mental health investments in the wake of COVID-19. WHO has previously highlighted the chronic underfunding of mental health: prior to the pandemic, countries were spending less than 2 per cent of their national health budgets on mental health, and struggling to meet their populations’ needs. And the pandemic is increasing demand for mental health services. Bereavement, isolation, loss of income and fear are triggering mental health conditions or exacerbating existing ones. Many people may be facing increased levels of alcohol and drug use, insomnia, and anxiety. Meanwhile, COVID-19 itself can lead to neurological and mental complications, such as delirium, agitation, and stroke. People with pre-existing mental, neurological or substance use disorders are also more vulnerable to SARS-CoV-2 infection ̶ they may stand a higher risk of severe outcomes and even death. “Good mental health is absolutely fundamental to overall health and well-being,” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of the World Health Organization. “COVID-19 has interrupted essential mental health services around the world just when they’re needed most. World leaders must move fast and decisively to invest more in life-saving mental health programmes ̶ during the pandemic and beyond.” Survey finds major disruptions to critical mental health services The survey was conducted from June to August 2020 among 130 countries across WHO’s six regions. It evaluates how the provision of mental, neurological and substance use services has changed due to COVID-19, the types of services that have been disrupted, and how countries are adapting to overcome these challenges. Countries reported widespread disruption of many kinds of critical mental health services: Over 60% reported disruptions to mental health services for vulnerable people, including children and adolescents (72%), older adults (70%), and women requiring antenatal or postnatal services (61%). 67% saw disruptions to counseling and psychotherapy; 65% to critical harm reduction services; and 45% to opioid agonist maintenance treatment for opioid dependence. More than a third (35%) reported disruptions to emergency interventions, including those for people experiencing prolonged seizures; severe substance use withdrawal syndromes; and delirium, often a sign of a serious underlying medical condition. 30% reported disruptions to access for medications for mental, neurological and substance use disorders. Around three-quarters reported at least partial disruptions to school and workplace mental health services (78% and 75% respectively). While many countries (70%) have adopted telemedicine or teletherapy to overcome disruptions to in-person services, there are significant disparities in the uptake of these interventions. More than 80% of high-income countries reported deploying telemedicine and teletherapy to bridge gaps in mental health, compared with less than 50% of low-income countries. WHO has issued guidance to countries on how to maintain essential services ̶ including mental health services ̶ during COVID-19 and recommends that countries allocate resources to mental health as an integral component of their response and recovery plans. The Organization also urges countries to monitor changes and disruptions in services so that they can address them as required. Although 89% of countries reported in the survey that mental health and psychosocial support is part of their national COVID-19 response plans, only 17% of these countries have full additional funding for covering these activities. This all highlights the need for more money for mental health. As the pandemic continues, even greater demand will be placed on national and international mental health programmes that have suffered from years of chronic underfunding. Spending 2% of national health budgets on mental health is not enough. International funders also need to do more: mental health still receives less than 1% of international aid earmarked for health. Those who do invest in mental health will reap rewards. Pre-COVID-19 estimates reveal that nearly US$ 1 trillion in economic productivity is lost annually from depression and anxiety alone. However, studies show that every US$ 1 spent on evidence-based care for depression and anxiety returns US$5. Note on World Mental Health Day: Mobilizing the global community to #MoveforMentalHeatlh On World Mental Health Day (Saturday 10 October), as part of its campaign Move for mental health: let’s invest , WHO is inviting the global community to take part in The Big Event for Mental Health , an unprecedented online advocacy event that will call for increased investment in mental health at all levels ̶ from individuals to businesses to countries to civil society ̶ so that the world can begin to close the gaps highlighted by today’s report. The Big Event is free and open to the public and will be broadcast on 10 October from 16:00 to 19:00 CEST on WHO’s YouTube, Facebook, Twitter, TikTok and LinkedIn channels and website. For updated information about the Big Event for Mental Health , including the latest lineup of performances and participants, visit the Big Event web page . To learn more about World Mental Health Day, visit WHO’s campaign page .

title: Global partnership to make available 120 million affordable, quality COVID-19 rapid tests for low- and middle-income countries
summary: A full access package includes WHO policy guidance on the use of antigen-based rapid diagnostic tests, manufacturer volume guarantees for low and middle-income countries, catalytic funding to assist governments to deploy the tests and an initial US$50 million procurement fund Several rapid, point-of-care antigen tests are being assessed by WHO for Emergency Use Listing (EUL) Agreements between the
content: A full access package includes WHO policy guidance on the use of antigen-based rapid diagnostic tests, manufacturer volume guarantees for low and middle-income countries, catalytic funding to assist governments to deploy the tests and an initial US$50 million procurement fund Several rapid, point-of-care antigen tests are being assessed by WHO for Emergency Use Listing (EUL) Agreements between the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation and test manufacturers Abbott and SD Biosensor make available innovative tests priced at a maximum of US$5 for low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) The Global Fund commits an initial US$50 million to enable countries to purchase the new tests, with the first orders expected to be placed this week Expedited market introduction of these tests in multiple LMICs is being supported through the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC), Unitaid, FIND, CHAI, and their partners This is the latest move from the Access to COVID-19 Tools (ACT) Accelerator to develop, procure and distribute critical new tools to fight the pandemic; new tests are urgently needed to meet the huge unmet needs for testing worldwide A set of agreements to make available, for low and middle-income countries, affordable, high-quality COVID-19 antigen rapid tests were today announced by the Access to COVID-19 Tools (ACT) Accelerator. Organizations involved in the milestone agreement include the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC), the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, the Clinton Health Access Initiative (CHAI), the Foundation for Innovative New Diagnostics (FIND), the Global Fund, Unitaid, and the World Health Organization (WHO). As part of this comprehensive, end-to-end effort, the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation has executed separate volume guarantee agreements with rapid diagnostic test (RDT) producers Abbott and SD Biosensor. These two arrangements will make available to LMICs 120 million antigen rapid diagnostic tests (Ag RDTs) – priced at a maximum of US$5 per unit – over a period of six months. These tests provide results in 15–30 minutes, rather than hours or days, and will enable expansion of testing, particularly in countries that do not have extensive laboratory facilities or trained health workers to implement molecular (polymerase-chain reaction or PCR) tests. The tests developed by Abbott and SD Biosensor are highly portable, reliable, and easy to administer, making testing possible in near-person, decentralized healthcare settings. Both companies’ tests are faster and cheaper than laboratory-based tests, enabling countries to increase the pace of testing, tracing and treating people for COVID-19 at the point of care particularly in areas with under-resourced health systems. A number of other Ag RDTs are at various stages of development and assessment. To scale up the Ag RDTs, the Global Fund today announced that it has made available an initial US$50 million from its COVID-19 Response Mechanism to enable countries to purchase at least 10 million of the new rapid tests for LMICs at the guaranteed price, with the first orders expected to be placed this week through the Global Fund’s pooled procurement mechanism. FIND and WHO are working together to accelerate appropriate use by supporting implementation research that will optimize Ag RDT use in multiple LMICs, in line with WHO guidance. This includes provision of catalytic volumes of tests to understand how Ag RDTs can best fit into health systems. Unitaid and Africa CDC will combine resources to initiate the roll out of these tests in up to 20 countries in Africa starting in October 2020. This multi-million-dollar intervention, currently undergoing final sign-off by their Boards, is designed to engage multiple partners active in the COVID-19 response in these countries, such as CHAI, African Society for Laboratory Medicine (ASLM) and local organizations. This will bolster efforts by the African Union’s Partnership to Accelerate COVID-19 Testing (PACT) initiative, launched in August 2020 to mobilize experts, community workers, supplies and other resources to minimize the impact of the pandemic on the African continent by testing, tracing, and treating COVID-19 cases in a timely manner. Testing is a critical cornerstone of the COVID-19 response, enabling countries to trace and contain the virus now, and to prepare for the roll-out of vaccines once available. Effective testing strategies rely on a portfolio of test types that can be used in different settings and situations. While molecular tests started to be rolled out within a month of the virus being sequenced, these tests are mainly laboratory based, relying on infrastructure and trained personnel to conduct them. Rapid tests to detect the presence of the virus at the point of care, which are faster and cheaper, are a vital addition to the testing arsenal needed to contain and fight COVID-19. WHO guidance published on 11 September 2020 highlights the value of these tests in areas where community transmission is widespread and where nucleic acid amplification-based diagnostic (NAAT) testing is either unavailable or where test results are significantly delayed. As well as supporting test-trace-isolate strategies, the tests can help identify or confirm new outbreaks, support outbreak investigations through screening; monitor disease trends; and potentially test asymptomatic contacts. The ACT-Accelerator Diagnostics Pillar is co-convened by FIND and the Global Fund, working closely with WHO and over 30 global health expert partners to accelerate innovation and overcome the technical, financial, and political obstacles to achieving equitable access to effective and timely testing. Such unprecedented global collaboration has enabled development and deployment of the first WHO EUL-approved Ag RDT within eight months of the first identification of the virus. In comparison, it took nearly five years to develop the first RDT for HIV. Several more antigen RDTs for COVID-19 are currently under WHO EUL review. Overall, the ACT-Accelerator Diagnostic Pillar aims to facilitate the supply of 500 million tests to LMICs within 12 months. These agreements are critical to fulfil the key objective of the ACT-Accelerator: to ensure all countries, regardless of income, have fair access to new tests and tools to fight COVID-19. The exceptional speed with which the Ag RDT access package has been created demonstrates the breadth of the impact of the ACT-Accelerator initiative, and this and future achievements in testing will complement similar milestones anticipated to emerge from the Vaccines and Therapeutics Pillars. Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus , Director General of WHO, said: “High-quality rapid tests show us where the virus is hiding, which is key to quickly tracing and isolating contacts and breaking the chains of transmission. The tests are a critical tool for governments as they look to reopen economies and ultimately save both lives and livelihoods.” Mark Suzman , Chief Executive Officer of the Gates Foundation, said: “Testing is an essential tool in the fight against COVID-19. We are delighted to join a partnership that will help ensure that the latest, high-quality diagnostics do not just go to the highest bidder but will be available at an affordable price to the world’s lower income countries. In addition, all of the actions announced today point to the growing success of the ACT-Accelerator in catalyzing global cooperation for a fair and effective response to this global crisis.” Dr Iain Barton , Chief Executive Officer of CHAI, said: “These agreements will help ensure that millions of people in low- and middle-income countries have access to high-quality rapid testing in villages and towns as well as cities. This has the potential to revolutionize government’s ability to respond to the pandemic, enabling quick diagnosis and response to contain localized virus outbreaks before they spread.” Andrea F. Wainer , Executive Vice President of Abbott’s rapid and molecular diagnostics businesses, said: “Abbott is pleased to bring our Panbio COVID-19 rapid antigen test and Sympheos digital solution to people and health authorities in low- and middle-income countries through this innovative partnership. We have long been committed to making sure our life-changing technologies are affordable and accessible, and for decades have been supporting many of these countries with our rapid tests for malaria, HIV, hepatitis, and other deadly infectious diseases.” Hyo-Keun Lee , Chief Executive Officer of SD Biosensor, said: “We, SD Biosensor, are pleased to supply our STANDARD Q COVID-19 rapid antigen tests for people who really need fast and accurate COVID-19 diagnosis. Through this partnership, we will keep striving do our best to provide the best quality of COVID-19 antigen rapid kits for fighting COVID-19.” Dr John Nkengasong , Director of the Africa CDC, said: “Antigen tests are an important complement to PCR testing, and are crucial to expand testing capacity throughout Africa. The beauty of antigen testing is that it is fast and gives quick results. It will allow healthcare workers to quickly isolate cases and treat them while tracing their contacts to cut the transmission chain.” Dr Philippe Duneton , Unitaid’s Executive Director a.i., said: “Access to these point-of-care rapid tests with be a game changer in the fight against COVID-19. We are working to support countries to rapidly deploy and use these new tests in the best possible way. Today’s news shows what the ACT-A partners working together can deliver in our efforts against the COVID-19 pandemic.” Dr Carolyn Gomes, Special Advisor for the Board, ProActividad, Jamaica, and Alternate Board Member (Developing Country NGOs), The Global Fund “Ensuring equitable access to rapid diagnostic tests is essential for controlling COVID-19 in all countries and to opening up economies across the world. Ensuring an affordable price is a major step forward. Tests that can be used at the point of care by front-line workers will greatly facilitate community access to testing. To ensure equity in access for those who need it most, there will need to be much greater support of the ACT-Accelerator and the Diagnostics Pillar in particular. Much more money is needed to meet the needs of the most vulnerable.” Peter Sands , Executive Director of the Global Fund, said: “This is the ACT-Accelerator in action. It is proof that by working together at a massive global scale, we can develop and deploy a vital new tool to help contain and fight the pandemic. This is not just a new test – it’s the money and the deployment plan to get it to where it’s needed, fast. This is the power of global collaboration.” Dr Catharina Boehme , Chief Executive Officer of FIND, said: “With this Ag RDT package, the ACT-Accelerator partners have secured much-needed tools for LMICs to dramatically increase COVID-19 testing. With the financial support of several countries, we have made great progress, but to ensure we reach all those who need testing and bring the prices down, we urgently need substantial funding from public, philanthropic, and multilateral sources.” About the ACT-Accelerator The Access to COVID-19 Tools (ACT) Accelerator, is a new, ground-breaking global collaboration to accelerate the development production, and equitable access to COVID-19 tests, treatments, and vaccines. It was set up in response to a call from G20 leaders in March 2020 and launched by WHO, the European Commission, France and the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation in April 2020. The ACT-Accelerator is not a decision-making body or a new organization, but works to speed up collaborative efforts among existing organizations to end the pandemic. It is a framework for collaboration that has been designed to bring key players around the table with the goal of ending the pandemic as quickly as possible through the accelerated development, equitable allocation, and scaled up delivery of tests, treatments and vaccines, thereby protecting health systems and restoring societies and economies in the near term. It draws on the experience of leading global health organizations which are tackling the world’s toughest health challenges, and who, by working together, are able to unlock new and more ambitious results against COVID-19. Its members share a commitment to ensure all people have access to all the tools needed to defeat COVID-19 and to work with unprecedented levels of partnership to achieve it. The ACT-Accelerator has four areas of work: diagnostics, therapeutics, vaccines and the health system connector. Cross-cutting all of these is the workstream on Access & Allocation. The Diagnostics Pillar of the ACT-Accelerator is focused on ensuring that everyone who needs a test can get one. Workstreams span research and development, market readiness, procurement, and country preparedness. Achievements to date include laboratory trainings in partnership with Africa CDC in early February, and a suite of online courses deployed within weeks. Nearly 20 million tests have been procured with the Diagnostics Consortium, ensuring diagnostic access for LMICs and readiness for test-and-treat implementation in these countries. Independent evaluations of antibody tests are also being conducted, as high-quality antibody tests are essential to understand population immunity for future vaccine roll out. content: The Coronavirus disease (COVID-19) is the first pandemic in history in which technology and social media are being used on a massive scale to keep people safe, informed, productive and connected. At the same time, the technology we rely on to keep connected and informed is enabling and amplifying an infodemic that continues to undermine the global response and jeopardizes measures to control the pandemic. An infodemic is an overabundance of information, both online and offline. It includes deliberate attempts to disseminate wrong information to undermine the public health response and advance alternative agendas of groups or individuals. Mis- and disinformation can be harmful to people’s physical and mental health; increase stigmatization; threaten precious health gains; and lead to poor observance of public health measures, thus reducing their effectiveness and endangering countries’ ability to stop the pandemic. Misinformation costs lives. Without the appropriate trust and correct information, diagnostic tests go unused, immunization campaigns (or campaigns to promote effective vaccines) will not meet their targets, and the virus will continue to thrive. Furthermore, disinformation is polarizing public debate on topics related to COVID-19; amplifying hate speech; heightening the risk of conflict, violence and human rights violations; and threatening long-terms prospects for advancing democracy, human rights and social cohesion. In this context, the UN Secretary- General launched the United Nations Communications Response initiative to combat the spread of mis- and disinformation in April 2020. The UN also issued a Guidance Note on Addressing and Countering COVID-19 related Hate Speech (11 May 2020). At the World Health Assembly in May 2020, WHO Member States passed Resolution WHA73.1 on the COVID-19 response. The Resolution recognizes that managing the infodemic is a critical part of controlling the COVID-19 pandemic: it calls on Member States to provide reliable COVID-19 content, take measures to counter mis- and disinformation and leverage digital technologies across the response. The Resolution also calls on international organizations to address mis- and disinformation in the digital sphere, work to prevent harmful cyber activities undermining the health response and support the provision of science-based data to the public. The UN system and civil society organizations are using their collective expertise and knowledge to respond to the infodemic. At the same time, as the pandemic continues to create uncertainty and anxiety, there is an urgent need for stronger action to manage the infodemic, and for a coordinated approach among states, multi-lateral organizations, civil society and all other actors who have a clear role and responsibility in combatting mis- and disinformation. We call on Member States to develop and implement action plans to manage the infodemic by promoting the timely dissemination of accurate information , based on science and evidence, to all communities, and in particular high-risk groups; and preventing the spread, and combating, mis- and disinformation while respecting freedom of expression. We urge Member States to engage and listen to their communities as they develop their national action plans , and to empower communities to develop solutions and resilience against mis- and disinformation. We further call on all other stakeholders - including the media and social media platforms through which mis- and disinformation are disseminated , researchers and technologists who can design and build effective strategies and tools to respond to the infodemic, civil society leaders and influencers - to collaborate with the UN system, with Member States and with each other, and to further strengthen their actions to disseminate accurate information and prevent the spread of mis- and disinformation.

title: WHO’s three messages for UNGA75
summary: As the world comes together at an unprecedented virtual session of the 75th UN General Assembly (UNGA), WHO has three messages to share.
content: As the world comes together at an unprecedented virtual session of the 75 th UN General Assembly (UNGA), WHO has three messages to share. The first is about equitable access to COVID-19 tools. At UNGA, WHO will call on world leaders to support the Access to COVID-19 Tools (ACT)-Accelerator, a unique international collaboration to fast-track the development, production and equitable access to COVID-19 tests, treatments, and vaccines globally, while strengthening health systems. Pooling investments globally, the ACT-Accelerator provides a chance for all countries to access a greater number of tools more quickly, sharing the risks and costs together. The ACT-Accelerator needs US$35 billion to fast-track the development, procurement and distribution of 2 billion vaccine doses, 245 million treatments and 500 million tests over the next year. The investment needed in a global solution aimed at equitable access pales in comparison to the economic impacts of COVID-19 and the domestic stimulus packages designed to keep economies afloat. Equitable access enables all countries to achieve full recovery by supporting all economic sectors, protecting the global value chain, and securing long-term global growth. The second message is about maintaining the momentum towards achieving the sustainable development goals. The pandemic risks unravelling decades of gains made in health and development. According to a recent WHO survey , 90% of countries are experiencing disruptions to essential health services due to the pandemic. The most frequently disrupted areas reported include routine immunization, non-communicable diseases diagnosis and treatment, family planning and contraception, treatment for mental health disorders, and cancer diagnosis and treatment. COVID-19 offers a stark reminder of why we need to invest in stronger health and data systems, rooted in primary healthcare, to achieve universal health coverage and to meet the health-related targets of the SDGs. The Global Action Plan for Healthy Lives and Well-being for All (GAP) works to accelerate country progress on the health-related targets of the SDGs, with the support of 12 multilateral agencies engaged in health, development and humanitarian response. This week we’ll learn about the progress made in laying the groundwork for a decade of delivery and action. Finally, we must prepare for the next pandemic together, now. COVID-19 has shown us that the world was woefully unprepared – despite the many warning signs and warnings. A year ago at UNGA, the independent Global Preparedness Monitoring Board (GPMB) warned of the threat of a pandemic, calling for global leaders to take urgent, united action to prepare. Earlier this week, the GPMB issued its 2020 report “World in disorder”. The report looks at a world disorientated by COVID-19, suffering from a lack of leadership and timely action. It calls for a renewed commitment to multilateralism and to WHO. At UNGA, WHO will call on all citizens and leaders to support the five actions outlined in the GPMB 2020 report: responsible leadership; engaged citizenship; strong and agile systems for health security; sustained investment and robust global governance of preparedness. Our actions today will define our collective future.

title: COVID-19 could reverse decades of progress toward eliminating preventable child deaths, agencies warn
